end: After Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P, Lectures 2 and 3
fine: Hornik 1991; Leshno et al. 1993; Vaswani et al. 2017; Hendrycks & Gimpel 2016; Ramachandran et al. 2017;
Dauphin et al. 2017; Shazeer 2020; Touvron et al. 2023; Groeneveld et al. 2024. The narration is a synthetic voice.
title: The Gate
From ReLU to SwiGLU
en.mm2: each new number: a weighted sum of the old ones
en.phi: Φ(x): the chance a bell-curve sample falls below x
en.who: BERT · the first GPT · GPT-2 code
en.cost: costs more than ReLU: still small change
en.silu2: the Sigmoid Linear Unit: in the 2016 GELU paper
en.srch2: a Google Brain team, combining simple functions
en.self: self-gated: x turns its own tap
en.pp2: same size, same compute; lower is better
en.par: each matrix entry: a weight, a parameter

cap.n0: Llama, Mistral and OLMo all run the same three-matrix trick.
cap.n1: And Llama and OLMo pay for it by|shrinking that layer to about two-thirds.|Why would anyone do that?
cap.n2: From Professor Yufei Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego:|the gate.
cap.n3: A matrix multiply turns a list of numbers|into a new list of weighted sums.
cap.n4: Layers like that are linear.|Stack as many as you like:|together they are still one matrix multiply.
cap.n5: One straight-line map, like straight rulers on a wavy curve.|Her class demo:
cap.c12: Instead of having two layers,|you can have three or five or six,|it doesn't really converge at all.
cap.n6: So between them goes a bend:|a non-linearity, also called an activation function.
cap.n7: In 1991, Kurt Hornik proved that one hidden layer,|with a bounded non-linear activation and enough units,
cap.n8: can get as close as you like to any|continuous function on a bounded region.|A 1993 follow-up covered ReLU too.
cap.n9: It promises that such a network exists,|not that training will find it.
cap.n10: Inside a transformer, the design behind these models,|the activation sits in one place:|the feed-forward layer. In her words:
cap.c17: The first layer is a matrix multiplication.|Right. The other one is also a matrix multiplication.
cap.n11: In letters: FFN of x equals act of x W1, times W2.
cap.n12: Each token, a word or a piece of one,|arrives as h numbers, the model width.|The first matrix widens it to 4h, the hidden width.
cap.n13: Picture the activation as a kitchen tap.|The water is the content.|The hand on the tap is the gate.
cap.n14: The 2017 Transformer used ReLU:|positive numbers pass as they are,|negative numbers become zero.
cap.n15: Shut or fully open: a switch.|Minus one goes in, zero comes out.
cap.n16: Training nudges each weight using slopes, called gradients.|ReLU's slope is one for positives, zero for negatives.
cap.n18: But if a unit outputs zero for every input,|its slope is zero everywhere.
cap.n19: No learning signal ever reaches it, so it never grows:|a dead ReLU.
cap.n20: So, a dimmer instead of a switch.|GELU multiplies x by Phi of x.
cap.n21: Phi of x is the chance a bell-curve sample falls below x:|near one for big x, near zero for very negative x.
cap.n22: The water sets the tap by itself:|a strong flow opens it, a negative trickle mostly shuts it.
cap.n23: Her slide 17, with our own curves.|Minus one now comes out as minus 0.16:|a trickle, so it still gets a gradient.
cap.n24: BERT and the first GPT used GELU.|It costs more than ReLU,|but beside the matrix multiplies it is small change.
cap.n25: A sigmoid squeezes any number into|an S-curve between zero and one.|Its slope never tops one quarter.
cap.c15: Sigmoid function itself is not good.
cap.n26: But as a hand on the tap, it works.|x times sigmoid of x: SiLU, the Sigmoid Linear Unit.
cap.n27: Cheaper than GELU: minus one comes out as minus 0.27.|And it was already in the 2016 GELU paper.
cap.n28: In 2017, a Google Brain team let a computer search|through combinations of simple functions.
cap.n29: Swish came out on top:|x times sigmoid of beta x.|With beta at one, it is exactly SiLU.
cap.n31: So far, the water turns its own tap:|the same x is both the water and the hand.
cap.n32: A gated linear unit gives the tap to a second person:|two separate matrix multiplies of the same input.
cap.n33: One makes the water.|A sigmoid of the other decides, number by number,|how much of that water gets through.
cap.c6: Instead of using the value for the gate|and the value for the value itself,|they are using two parts.|One is just for the gating|and the other one is just for the value.
cap.n34: SwiGLU, Swish plus GLU, gives that hand a SiLU:|SiLU of x W, times x V, then W2.
cap.n35: Three matrices: one makes the gate, one makes the content,|one brings the result back down.
cap.n36: On her slide 20, the pen fixes one word:|SwiGLU's gate is SiLU, as the figure on her own slide says.
cap.n37: Llama, Mistral and OLMo all use SwiGLU.|Gemma uses a GELU-gated cousin, GeGLU.
cap.n38: Her slide 21 keeps score.|Cheap forward? Cheap gradient?|ReLU: yes, yes. GELU: no, no. SiLU: so-so.
cap.n39: Healthy gradients? Not ReLU. And her last row:|today's winners run SiLU, mostly as SwiGLU,|like Llama, Mistral and OLMo.
cap.n40: Better, but only a little:|about 1.68 against 1.64 on the paper's score,|lower is better.
cap.n41: And why does it work? The paper ends:
cap.n42: “We offer no explanation as to why|these architectures seem to work;|we attribute their success,|as all else, to divine benevolence.”
cap.c7: A lot of research is experimental research.|If you get better results, you can get good explanation.
cap.c8: No one will know which one is better until you test it.
cap.n43: Now the bill.|Each matrix entry is a weight the model learns, a parameter.
cap.n44: A plain layer: two matrices of h by 4h, 8 h-squared weights.|A third one at the same width makes 12 h-squared.
cap.n45: Each weight costs about two operations per token,|a multiply and an add.|More weights, more compute.
cap.c20: Instead of having four times,|maybe we need to have a different dimension.
cap.n46: Three matrices of h by the new width|hold 3 times h times that width.|Set that equal to 8 h-squared.
cap.n47: The new width comes out at 8 thirds of h:|two-thirds of 4h, about 2.67 h.|Same weights, same compute.
cap.n48: In Llama's 7B model, 4h would be 16,384.|Two-thirds is about 10,923; the code rounds up to 11,008.|OLMo's 7B lands on the same 11,008.
cap.n49: Back to the puzzle: one matrix for the water,|one for the hand, one for the way back.
cap.n50: A switch, then a dimmer, then a second pair of hands.
